Efficient Representation of multicategorical local Hilbert spaces: nonlinear Restricted Boltzmann Machines to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks

Abhiroop Lahiri Email: scsal3480@iacs.res.in Affiliation: School of Chemical Sciences, Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Kolkata, India
Abstract

Neural network quantum states (NQS) for representing spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} systems are typically built from Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with binary visible variables, in which the input spins are first combined through linear affine maps before more expressive nonlinear transformations are applied. And the standard way for representing multi-categorical systems, namely spin-11 and 22, or the q-state quantum Potts systems, i.e. with more than 2-local degrees of freedom, is a unary or one-hot encoded MLP architecture. Following a few similar studies, I observe that while the one-hot construction is the mathematically faithful encoding for systems with more than two local states such as spin-SS models with S>12S\!>\!\tfrac{1}{2} or qq-state Potts models, its parameter count grows with the number of local states, and the resulting optimization landscape can hinder convergence. I find numerically, that allowing log⁡Ψ\log\Psi to be a nonlinear function of the raw multi-valued spin variable is a natural categorical generalization: it preserves the labelling freedom of the local basis and reproduces the one-hot model with strictly fewer parameters, often at improved trainability. I first benchmark this idea on shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), equipping them with several distinct nonlinear connections, for spin-11, 22, and 33 Heisenberg chains. I then turn to Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks(KANs), edge carrying a learnable univariate nonlinearity, and show that they provide a strictly more expressive realization of the same principle. Finally, I demonstrate that this framework captures the critical behaviour of the quantum Potts Hamiltonian, recovering its phase transition.

I Introduction

Quantum many-body systems with strong correlations remain among the most demanding computational problems in condensed matter physics. The ‘curse of dimensionality’ that is, exponential growth of the Hilbert space with system size makes exact treatment infeasible beyond modest sizes, motivating the development of compressed and stochastic representations: Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) [26] and the broader family of matrix product and tensor network states, and Quantum Monte Carlo methods. Each of these has well-known strengths and equally well-known limitations: dimensionality or entanglement constraints, fermion sign problems, or the difficulty of designing accurate trial wave functions.

Over the past decade, machine-learning architectures have emerged as a flexible alternative for representing many-body wave functions [18, 8, 15, 2, 7, 6, 10]. The seminal work of Carleo and Troyer [1] introduced the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) as a variational ansatz for quantum spin systems, and the broader paradigm of neural network quantum states (NQS) has since produced competitive results on a range of spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} quantum many-body Hamiltonians using RBMs, convolutional networks [3], recurrent and autoregressive networks [11], and transformer-based architectures[27, 25]. A common feature of nearly all of these constructions is that the visible degrees of freedom are taken to be binary, and the log-amplitude log⁡Ψ\log\Psi is a composition of linear (or affine) in those visible inputs before being passed through a nonlinear hidden-layer activation functions.

This linearity in the visible variable is not a neutral choice. For spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} it is invisible, because the local Hilbert space has only two states and any pair of labels {μ,ν}\{\mu,\nu\} can be mapped to any other by an affine transformation; the labelling freedom of the RBM weights and biases absorbs the re-labelling exactly, as pointed out by Pei et. al [17]. As soon as the local Hilbert space contains three or more states, such as in spin-11, spin-32\tfrac{3}{2}, spin-22, or in qq-state Potts models, this freedom is lost. Treating the state as a number forces the neural network to assume an artificial ordering between those states (e.g., −S<−S+1<⋯<S-S<-S\!+\!1<\dots<S in case of spins). This introduces a notion of distance or “closeness” between states that has no physical meaning, and as a result, it unnecessarily restricts the kinds of wave functions the model can represent.

While standard one-hot encoding maps the (2​S+1)(2S+1) local spin states to binary indicator variables to restore basis-relabeling invariance, it increases visible-to-hidden parameter counts. A more economical alternative is to retain a single scalar variable per site and allow log⁡Ψ\log\Psi to depend nonlinearly on it. Because any function over a discrete dd-valued domain can be exactly represented by a polynomial of degree at most d−1d-1, this nonlinear encoding spans the exact same function space as one-hot encoding rather than approximating it, thus providing a strictly more compact basis. This is the observation that underlies the nonlinear-RBM ansatz of Pei and Clark [17], and, as I will argue, it naturally generalizes to architectures with learnable edge nonlinearities, such as Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) [13].

The purpose of this paper is to make this design principle explicit and to test it across two kinds of architectures:

  1. 1.

    Restricted Boltzmann Machines with nonlinear energy functions. I benchmark four types nonlinear RBMs, with both monomial and Chebyshev expansions, as well as sinusoidal functions of of the visible variable, against one-hot RBMs on spin-22 (having 5 local spin degrees of freedom per site) , spin-33 (7 local states per site) and 33 Heisenberg chains.

  2. 2.

    Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Rather than fixing a polynomial basis a priori, each edge of the network learns its own univariate function. I show that KANs acting on raw spin inputs outperform one-hot encoded MLPs of comparable parameter count on the 24-site spin-11 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions, and I apply the same architecture to the one-dimensional q=5q\!=\!5 quantum Potts model in a transverse field, recovering the first-order quantum phase transition and subsequently showing a downward trend when performed supervised learning with the with reference DMRG ground states.

I use the spectrum of the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) matrix as a quantitative diagnostic in both the cases, of how well the parameter space is conditioned by each ansatz. Taken together, these results identify nonlinearity in the categorical visible variable, hand how wll these network ansatze perform when applied to general-spin and Potts Hamiltonians.

II Nonlinear log-amplitudes for categorical variables

I begin by formalizing the design principle that motivates the rest of the paper.

II.1 Labelling freedom and the categorical obstruction

Let me consider a many-body wave function Ψ⁡(𝝈)\Psi(\bm{\sigma}) on a lattice of NN sites, where each σi\sigma_{i} takes values in a discrete local degree of freedom 𝒜\mathcal{A} with |𝒜|=d|\mathcal{A}|=d. For spin-SS, 𝒜={−S,−S+1,…,S−1,S}\mathcal{A}=\{-S,-S\!+\!1,\dots,S\!-\!1,S\} and d=2​S+1d\!=\!2S\!+\!1. For qq-state Potts, 𝒜={0,1,…,q−1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1,\dots,q\!-\!1\} and d=qd\!=\!q. Physical observables depend only on Ψ\Psi as a function on 𝒜N\mathcal{A}^{N}, not on the particular numerical labels assigned to the elements of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Any reasonable variational ansatz Ψθ\Psi_{\theta} should therefore be invariant, up to a redefinition of its parameters θ\theta, under arbitrary relabellings of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

For d=2d\!=\!2 (spin-12\tfrac{1}{2}, Ising), as pointed out in the paper by Pei and clark [17] this property is automatic for any architecture in which log⁡Ψθ\log\Psi_{\theta} is affine in the visible input σi\sigma_{i}, because any two pairs of labels are related by an affine transformation σ→α​σ+β\sigma\to\alpha\sigma+\beta that can be absorbed into a rescaling of the weights and a shift of the biases. This is precisely why the standard RBM works as well as it does for spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} models.

For d≥3d\!\geq\!3, no such absorption is possible. An ansatz that is linear in σi\sigma_{i} implicitly equips 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the affine structure of ℝ\mathbb{R}, which is physically meaningless: the spin labels in spin-11 are not a priori “one apart”, and the labels in the qq-state Potts model are not ordered at all. This is the categorical obstruction to lifting binary NQS to higher local dimensions.

II.2 Two resolutions

There are two ways to restore label invariance for d≥3d\!\geq\!3.

One-hot encoding.

If I replace each scalar visible variable σi\sigma_{i} by a dd-dimensional binary vector 𝒗i​(σi)∈{0,1}d\bm{v}_{i}(\sigma_{i})\in\{0,1\}^{d} with a single nonzero entry. An affine function of 𝒗i\bm{v}_{i} is automatically invariant under arbitrary relabellings of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, because any function on a dd-element set can be written as an affine function of its indicator vector. This is the construction underlying the softmax RBM [14] and the one-hot encoded MLP.

Nonlinear scalar encoding.

Alternatively, I can keep a single scalar input σi∈𝒜\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{A}, but allow log⁡Ψθ\log\Psi_{\theta} to depend on σi\sigma_{i} through a nonlinear map of degree ≥d−1\geq d\!-\!1. Concretely, any function f:𝒜→ℝf:\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} on a dd-element set is a polynomial in σ\sigma of degree at most d−1d\!-\!1, since the dd monomials 1,σ,σ2,…,σd−11,\sigma,\sigma^{2},\dots,\sigma^{d-1} span the function space on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Equivalently, one may use any other basis of degree ≤d−1\leq d\!-\!1, e.g. Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind on [−1,1][-1,1] after rescaling σi→σi/S\sigma_{i}\to\sigma_{i}/S.

Although the two resolutions are not representationally equivalent on the local Hilbert space, they are sometimes advantageous due to (i) the lesser parameter count (ii) better conditioning of the optimization problem, and (iii) the inductive bias they impose on cross-site correlations through hidden-layer activations.

II.3 Restricted Boltzmann Machines with nonlinear connections

The nonlinear RBM (RBMpow) of Pei and Clark [17], in turn suggested by Das Sarma and collaborators [7], is a concrete realization of the nonlinear scalar encoding. Its unnormalized amplitude is

ΨRBMp​o​w​(𝝈)\displaystyle\Psi_{\mathrm{RBM}_{pow}}(\bm{\sigma}) =∑{hj}exp[∑n=1nmax∑i​jWi​j(n)σinhj\displaystyle=\sum_{\{h_{j}\}}\exp\Bigl[\,\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{ij}W^{(n)}_{ij}\,\sigma_{i}^{n}\,h_{j}
+∑n=1nmax∑iai(n)σin+∑jhjbj],\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{i}a^{(n)}_{i}\,\sigma_{i}^{n}+\sum_{j}h_{j}b_{j}\Bigr], (1)

where the hidden units hjh_{j} are summed out analytically as in the standard RBM, yielding a closed-form log⁡ΨRBMpow\log\Psi_{\mathrm{RBM_{pow}}} that is a sum of softplus terms applied to polynomials of degree nmaxn_{\max} in the visible inputs. It uses the spin directly as the scalar features per site rather than dd binary ones, it does not split each hidden-unit contribution across dd separate weights Choosing nmax≥d−1n_{\max}\geq d\!-\!1 guarantees full expressivity on the local state, and the labelling freedom is restored exactly.

For the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} case, d−1=1d\!-\!1=1 and Eq. (1) collapses to the original RBM. For d≥3d\!\geq\!3 the additional terms σi2,σi3,…\sigma_{i}^{2},\sigma_{i}^{3},\dots are not optional refinements but the minimal extension required to remove the categorical obstruction.

II.4 Chebyshev basis

To investigate whether there can be better conditioning in such nonlinear RBMs, I have considered a second variant, which I call the Chebyshev RBM (RBMChe), in which σin\sigma_{i}^{n} in Eq.(1) is replaced by Tn​(σi/S)T_{n}(\sigma_{i}/S), with TnT_{n} the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind:

ΨRBMC​h​e​(𝝈)\displaystyle\Psi_{\mathrm{RBM}_{Che}}(\bm{\sigma}) =∑{hj}exp[∑n=1nmax∑i​jWi​j(n)Tn(σi/S)hj\displaystyle=\sum_{\{h_{j}\}}\exp\Bigl[\,\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{ij}W^{(n)}_{ij}\,T_{n}(\sigma_{i}/S)\,h_{j}
+∑n=1nmax∑iai(n)Tn(σi/S)+∑jhjbj].\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{i}a^{(n)}_{i}\,T_{n}(\sigma_{i}/S)+\sum_{j}h_{j}b_{j}\Bigr]. (2)

Equations (1) and (2) define the same function space on 𝒜N\mathcal{A}^{N}. The usage of Chebyshev polynomials for approximating smooth functions on [−1,1][-1,1] is well known in classical numerical analysis. Although these are discrete functions of As I verify in Sec. IV, in some cases, the Chebyshev parameterization yields a better-conditioned SR matrix and improved variational accuracy at fixed parameter count.

II.5 Sinusoidal basis

I consider a sinusoidal parameterisation of the nonlinear RBM edge activation inspired by the SineKAN architecture [19]. In SineKAN, the learnable univariate function on each edge of the Kolmogorov–Arnold network is expanded as a finite sum of sine functions,

φi​j​(xj)=∑k=1GAi​j​k​sin⁡(ωk​xj+ψj​k)\varphi_{ij}(x_{j})=\sum_{k=1}^{G}A_{ijk}\,\sin\!\bigl(\omega_{k}\,x_{j}+\psi_{jk}\bigr) (3)

where Ai​j​kA_{ijk} are per-edge amplitudes, ωk\omega_{k} are frequencies shared across all edges, and ψj​k\psi_{jk} are per-input-node phases. Within the nonlinear RBM framework, this amounts to replacing the polynomial or Chebyshev visible-unit functions {fp​(σi)}\{f_{p}(\sigma_{i})\} with a set of GG sinusoidal channels evaluated on the normalised spin variable σ¯i=σi/2​S\bar{\sigma}_{i}=\sigma_{i}/2S. In terms of the powers of σ\sigma, the this basis will have all powers when the sine is expanded. The amplitude of this ansatz then takes the form

Ψ⁡(𝝈)=∏μ2​cosh⁡[∑k=1G∑i=1NAμ​i​k​sin⁡(ωk​σ¯i+ψi​k)+bμ]\displaystyle\Psi(\bm{\sigma})=\prod_{\mu}2\cosh\!\Biggl[\sum_{k=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{N}A_{\mu ik}\,\sin\!\bigl(\omega_{k}\,\bar{\sigma}_{i}+\psi_{ik}\bigr)+b_{\mu}\Biggr]
×exp⁡[∑k=1Gvk​∑i=1Nsin⁡(ωk(v)​σ¯i+ψk(v))]\displaystyle\times\exp\!\Biggl[\sum_{k=1}^{G}v_{k}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sin\!\bigl(\omega_{k}^{(v)}\,\bar{\sigma}_{i}+\psi_{k}^{(v)}\bigr)\Biggr] (4)

where translational symmetry is imposed on the hidden-layer weights by the standard permutation-equivariant construction and on the visible bias by using site-independent amplitudes vkv_{k}, frequencies ωk(v)\omega_{k}^{(v)}, and phases ψk(v)\psi_{k}^{(v)}. A key advantage of the sine basis over power series and the Chebyshev bases is that the number of basis functions GG is a free hyperparameter independent of the local Hilbert space dimension d=2​S+1d=2S+1: the same architecture applies without modification across all spin values, and GG can be tuned to balance expressibility against the conditioning of the quantum geometric tensor during optimization.

II.6 Other bases: B-splines

A natural alternative to the global monomials σin\sigma_{i}^{n} or Chebyshev polynomials Tn​(σi/S)T_{n}(\sigma_{i}/S) is a locally supported basis. B-splines of degree pp generated from a knot vector {t0,…,tm}\{t_{0},\dots,t_{m}\} via the Cox-de-Boor recursion[5]. The corresponding RBMspl ansatz is obtained from Eq. (1) by the replacement σin→Bn(p)​(σi/S)\sigma_{i}^{n}\to B^{(p)}_{n}(\sigma_{i}/S). The B-spline construction is, however, ill-suited to the higher-spin problem for a structural reason. Resolving all dd categorical spin values requires nmax=d−1n_{\max}=d-1 basis functions; with a clamped knot vector on [−1,1][-1,1] this forces the degree to p=d−2p=d-2. Each Bn(p)B^{(p)}_{n} is then a piecewise polynomial of degree d−2d-2 in σi\sigma_{i}, whereas the exact reconstruction of dd distinct spin-dependent amplitudes requires polynomial degree d−1d-1, as already provided by the monomial and Chebyshev parameterizations. The function spaces therefore no longer coincide, and RBMspl represents a strictly smaller variational manifold than the polynomial variants at fixed nmaxn_{\max}. So I do not pursue B-splines further and restrict our comparison to the power series, Chebyshev and sinusoidal bases.

II.7 Translational equivariance of the of the general nonlinear RBMs

Any such nonlinear RBM ansatze (5) is exactly invariant under lattice translations for any choice of the basis functions {ℱn}\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\}, provided the weight tensors are symmetrized by the standard permutation-equivariant construction.

If I consider a periodic chain of NN sites with the cyclic translation group 𝒯={Tg}g=0N−1\mathcal{T}=\{T_{g}\}_{g=0}^{N-1}, where TgT_{g} shifts every site index by gg modulo NN. After tracing out the hidden units, the log-amplitude takes the form

ln⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈)\displaystyle\ln\Psi(\bm{\sigma}) =∑jρ⁡(∑n=1nmax∑i=1NWi​j(n)​ℱn​(σi/S)+bj)\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\rho\!\Biggl(\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{(n)}_{ij}\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\!\bigl(\sigma_{i}/S\bigr)+b_{j}\Biggr)
+∑n=1nmax∑i=1Nai(n)ℱ~n(σi/S),\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a^{(n)}_{i}\,\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{n}\!\bigl(\sigma_{i}/S\bigr)\,, (5)

where ρ=logcosh\rho=\log\cosh and jj runs over hidden units. I treat the hidden and visible contributions in turn.
The permutation-equivariant construction replaces the free weight Wi​j(n)W^{(n)}_{ij} by a symmetry-expanded kernel: a single tensor Wf,i(n)W^{(n)}_{f,i} of shape (hidden ×\times sites) is stored, and the pre-activation at hidden index ff and symmetry index gg is defined as

θf,g​(𝝈)=∑n=1nmax∑i=1NWf,Tg​(i)(n)​ℱn​(σi/S)+bf\theta_{f,g}(\bm{\sigma})\;=\;\sum_{n=1}^{n_{\max}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{(n)}_{f,\,T_{g}(i)}\;\mathcal{F}_{n}\!\bigl(\sigma_{i}/S\bigr)+b_{f} (6)

Under a translation ThT_{h} of the input, σi→σTh−1​(i)\sigma_{i}\to\sigma_{T_{h}^{-1}(i)}:

θf,g​(Th​𝝈)=∑n∑iWf,Tg​(i)(n)​ℱn​(σTh−1​(i)/S)+bf\theta_{f,g}(T_{h}\,\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{n}\sum_{i}W^{(n)}_{f,\,T_{g}(i)}\;\mathcal{F}_{n}\!\bigl(\sigma_{T_{h}^{-1}(i)}/S\bigr)+b_{f} (7)

Re-indexing the site sum by setting i′=Th−1​(i)i^{\prime}=T_{h}^{-1}(i), I get i=Th​(i′)i=T_{h}(i^{\prime}) and Tg​(i)=Tg∘Th​(i′)=Tg+h​(i′)T_{g}(i)=T_{g}\circ T_{h}(i^{\prime})=T_{g+h}(i^{\prime}). Since ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} is a univariate function of the local spin variable(the same function applied identically at every site) it is insensitive to this re-labelling:

θf,g​(Th​𝝈)​Wf,Tg+h​(i′)(n)​ℱn​(σi′/S)+bf\displaystyle\theta_{f,g}(T_{h}\,\bm{\sigma})W^{(n)}_{f,\,T_{g+h}(i^{\prime})}\;\mathcal{F}_{n}\!\bigl(\sigma_{i^{\prime}}/S\bigr)+b_{f} =θf,g+h​(𝝈).\displaystyle=\theta_{f,\,g+h}(\bm{\sigma})\,. (8)

The hidden-layer contribution to the log-amplitude sums over all features ff and symmetry indices gg:

∑f∑g=0N−1ρ⁡(θf,g​(Th​𝝈))\displaystyle\sum_{f}\sum_{g=0}^{N-1}\rho\!\bigl(\theta_{f,g}(T_{h}\,\bm{\sigma})\bigr) =∑f∑g=0N−1ρ⁡(θf,g+h​(𝝈))\displaystyle=\sum_{f}\sum_{g=0}^{N-1}\rho\!\bigl(\theta_{f,\,g+h}(\bm{\sigma})\bigr)
=∑f∑g′=0N−1ρ⁡(θf,g′​(𝝈)),\displaystyle=\sum_{f}\sum_{g^{\prime}=0}^{N-1}\rho\!\bigl(\theta_{f,g^{\prime}}(\bm{\sigma})\bigr)\,, (9)

where the last equality is a re-indexing of a complete sum over ℤN\mathbb{Z}_{N}. The hidden-layer contribution is therefore exactly invariant.

Parameter reduction.

Beyond guaranteeing the correct quantum numbers, the permutation-equivariant construction yields a substantial reduction in the number of variational parameters. Without symmetry, each basis channel nn requires an independent weight matrix Wj​i(n)W^{(n)}_{ji} of size M×NM\times N, where MM is the total number of hidden units. The hidden-layer cost is therefore nmax×M×Nn_{\max}\times M\times N parameters. In the equivariant construction the MM hidden units factorise as M=F×NsymmM=F\times N_{\mathrm{symm}}, where F=⌊α​N/Nsymm⌋F=\lfloor\alpha\,N/N_{\mathrm{symm}}\rfloor is the number of independent features and Nsymm=|𝒯|=NN_{\mathrm{symm}}=|\mathcal{T}|=N for the full translation group of a periodic chain. Each channel stores only an F×NF\times N kernel that is reused across all NsymmN_{\mathrm{symm}} translations, reducing the hidden-layer parameter count to nmax×F×Nn_{\max}\times F\times N. The overall reduction factor is

nmax​M​Nnmax​F​N=MF=Nsymm,\frac{n_{\max}\,M\,N}{n_{\max}\,F\,N}\;=\;\frac{M}{F}\;=\;N_{\mathrm{symm}}\,, (10)

i.e. the number of hidden-layer parameters decreases by exactly the order of the symmetry group, independent of the choice of basis functions {ℱn}\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\} or their number nmaxn_{\max}.

II.8 Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks as learnable nonlinear encodings

Both Eqs. (1) and (2), and general nonlinear RBMs mentioned above, fix the per-site nonlinear basis a priori. A natural further step is to let the network learn the per-site nonlinearity itself. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) [13] do exactly this: in contrast to an MLP, where every edge carries a scalar weight and every node carries a fixed activation, in a KAN every edge i→ji\to j carries a learnable univariate function ϕj​i​(⋅)\phi_{ji}(\cdot), typically parameterized as a B-spline (or, in the variants I use here, as a sinusoidal basis functions), and node values are obtained by summing the edge contributions:

xj(ℓ+1)=∑iϕj​i(ℓ)​(xi(ℓ)).x_{j}^{(\ell+1)}\;=\;\sum_{i}\phi^{(\ell)}_{ji}\!\left(x_{i}^{(\ell)}\right). (11)

For categorical inputs σi∈𝒜\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{A}, a KAN with a single hidden layer is capable of implementing the nonlinear scalar encoding described above: the first-layer univariate functions ϕj​i(0)\phi^{(0)}_{ji} are evaluated only on the dd points of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and span an arbitrary function on the local state. KANs therefore generalize the RBMpow and RBMChe constructions in a precise sense: they replace the fixed polynomial basis {Tn​(σ/S)}\{T_{n}(\sigma/S)\} by a basis whose coefficients and shape are jointly optimized together with the rest of the network. I exploit this in Secs. V and VI.

III Variational Monte Carlo and Stochastic Reconfiguration

For all of the architectures considered in this paper I use Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) to the variational energy E⁡[θ]=⟨Ψθ|H|Ψθ⟩/⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩E[\theta]=\langle\Psi_{\theta}|H|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle/\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle. The energy expectation value is written as

E⁡[θ]=⟨⟨Eloc⟩⟩,Eloc​(𝒙)=∑𝒙′H𝒙​𝒙′​Ψθ​(𝒙′)Ψθ​(𝒙),E[\theta]\;=\;\langle\!\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}\rangle\!\rangle,\qquad E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{x})\;=\;\sum_{\bm{x}^{\prime}}H_{\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\prime}}\,\frac{\Psi_{\theta}(\bm{x}^{\prime})}{\Psi_{\theta}(\bm{x})}, (12)

and estimated by Markov-chain sampling of |Ψθ​(𝒙)|2|\Psi_{\theta}(\bm{x})|^{2}. The parameters θ\theta are updated by stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [22]:

Δ​θ=γ​(S+ϵ​𝟙)−1​𝒇,\Delta\theta\;=\;\gamma\,(S+\epsilon\mathbb{1})^{-1}\bm{f}, (13)

where Sl​l′=⟨Δl​Δl′⟩−⟨Δl⟩​⟨Δl′⟩S_{ll^{\prime}}=\langle\Delta_{l}\Delta_{l^{\prime}}\rangle-\langle\Delta_{l}\rangle\langle\Delta_{l^{\prime}}\rangle is the (real part of the) quantum geometric tensor, fl=⟨Δl​H⟩−⟨Δl⟩​⟨H⟩f_{l}=\langle\Delta_{l}H\rangle-\langle\Delta_{l}\rangle\langle H\rangle, and Δl=∂llog⁡Ψθ\Delta_{l}=\partial_{l}\log\Psi_{\theta}. I use a diagonal shift ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3} throughout, and I monitor the full spectrum of SS as a diagnostic of the conditioning of the optimization landscape. All RBM and KAN experiments below are implemented on top of NetKet [23] with custom modules for the nonlinear and KAN ansatze.

The Hamiltonians considered are the antiferromagnetic spin-SS Heisenberg chain

HHeis=∑⟨i​j⟩[Siz​Sjz+12​(Si+​Sj−+Si−​Sj+)]H_{\mathrm{Heis}}\;=\;\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\!\left[\,S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(S^{+}_{i}S^{-}_{j}+S^{-}_{i}S^{+}_{j}\right)\!\right] (14)

and the one-dimensional qq-state quantum Potts model in a transverse field

HPotts=−J∑⟨i​j⟩∑k=1q−1ΩikΩjq−k−Γ∑i∑k=1q−1Xik,H_{\mathrm{Potts}}\;=\;-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}\Omega_{i}^{k}\,\Omega_{j}^{q-k}\;-\;\Gamma\sum_{i}\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}X_{i}^{k}, (15)

where Ωi\Omega_{i} is the stantard ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q} clock operator Ωi=diag⁡(1,ω,ω2,…,ωq−1)\Omega_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\,\omega,\,\omega^{2},\,\ldots,\,\omega^{q-1}), where ωk=e2​π​k/q\omega^{k}=e^{2\pi k/q} are the qq the roots of unity. XiX_{i} are the shift (cyclic permutation) operators acting on the qq-dimensional local Hilbert space at site ii and X​|k⟩=|(k+1)modq⟩X|k\rangle=|(k+1)\bmod q\rangle. I work throughout with q=5q=5, open boundary conditions, and I use Γ/J\Gamma/J as the tuning parameter. For q≥5q\geq 5 the transition driven by Γ/J\Gamma/J is known to be of first order [21].

IV Restricted Boltzmann Machine benchmarks

I first verify the framework of Sec. II on the nonlinear RBMs. All ansätze were implemented in JAX and Flax libraries in Python with the VMC optimization carried out using the NetKet library [23]. Exact-diagonalization reference values were obtained from an in-house ED code, while the DMRG benchmarks were computed using the ITensor library [9]. All the calculations were executed in the 16 GB T4 GPU facilty of Google Colab.

For each system I compare the 3 RBM ansatze with the same hidden-unit densities α=M/N\alpha=M/N: (i) the one-hot RBM, (ii) the polynomial nRBM Throughout this section the total SzS^{z} is fixed to zero, the sector in which the Heisenberg ground state lives, and reference energies are obtained by exact diagonalization (ED) and DMRG. All systems use periodic boundary conditions and translational symmetry. Adding lattice translation symmetry to the ansatz [3, 24] and reduces the parameter count of both ansatze by a factor of NN and preserves their relative ordering.

IV.1 Spin-22 and 33 chains: all the nonlinear RBM architectures

I begin by benchmarking the three nonlinear RBM ansatze, RBMpow, RBMChe and RBMsin on the antiferromagnetic spin-2 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions. For each ansatz and each value of the hidden density α\alpha, I perform VMC optimization using SR and report the relative error ϵ=(EVMC−Eexact)/|Eexact|\epsilon=(E_{\mathrm{VMC}}-E_{\mathrm{exact}})/|E_{\mathrm{exact}}| of the converged ground-state energy with respect to the exact value obtained from DMRG. For spin-22 nmax=4n_{\max}=4 and for spin-33 nmax=6n_{\max}=6 basis functions per channel, translational symmetry is imposed via the permutation-equivariant construction derived in Sec. II.7, and the remaining hyperparameters (learning rate=0.001=0.001, number of samples=20482048, diagonal shift=0.006=0.006) are held fixed across runs to ensure a fair comparison.

Figure 1(a) shows the relative error as a function of hidden density for the spin-2 chain. At α=1\alpha=1 the three ansatze perform comparably, with relative errors of approximately 2%2\%. As α\alpha increases, clear differences emerge: the Chebyshev RBM converges most rapidly, reaching a relative error below 10−310^{-3} by α=4\alpha=4, while the RBMpow follows a similar trajectory but saturates at a slightly higher floor of roughly 1.5×10−31.5\times 10^{-3}. The sine RBM, by contrast, plateaus near 4×10−34\times 10^{-3} for α≥3\alpha\geq 3 and shows no appreciable improvement with further increases in hidden density. However, the ordering changes for the spin-3 chain [Fig. 1(b)]: the RBMpow now achieves the lowest error, reaching ∼10−3{\sim}10^{-3} at α=4\alpha=4, while the RBMChe, which dominated at spin-2, stalls at a bit higher error with substantially larger run-to-run variance. The RBMsin improves relative to its spin-2 performance and reaches errors comparable to Chebyshev at large α\alpha. This reversal indicates that no single basis is uniformly optimal across all local Hilbert space dimensions.

To understand the origin of these differences, I examine the spectrum of the SR matrix, also known as the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) at convergence. Panels (c)–(e) of Fig. 1 show histograms of log10⁡λ\log_{10}\lambda, where λ\lambda are the eigenvalues of the QGT, for each spin-2 ansatz at α=5\alpha=5. The eigenvalues of the SR matrix quantify the curvature of log⁡Ψθ\log\Psi_{\theta} along the corresponding parameter-space directions [4, 16]. Small eigenvalues correspond to “flat” directions where SR updates are aggressively rescaled by the regularized inverse and effectively become noise-dominated. A spectrum tightly clustered near the top eigenvalue indicates that all directions in parameter space carry comparable information, which is the regime in which SR is best ’behaved’. Although all the RBMs exhibit eigenvalues spanning ten orders of magnitude or more, the RBMChe has the most symmetric structure and least spread reflecting moderate the best conditioning. Also, the RBMpow also showing good clustering but less density of eigenvalues from 10010^{0} to 10510^{5} than shows moderate conditioning. The RBMpow [panel (e)] has the widest spread, with eigenvalues extending from ∼10−7{\sim}10^{-7} to ∼10−5{\sim}10^{-5} (with a few values at machine precision)

a condition number(ratio of the highest to the lowest eigenvalues) exceeding 101210^{12}. The presence of significant weight at large eigenvalues indicates that the sinusoidal basis introduces stiff directions in parameter space that limit convergence. The spin-3 spectra [panels (f)-(h)] reveal why the Chebyshev advantage erodes at larger local Hilbert space dimension: its eigenvalue spread widens further and the regularization can no longer compensate, leading to the degraded performance and larger error bars seen in panel (b). The power-series spectrum, by contrast, remains comparatively stable across spins, consistent with its more robust convergence at spin-3.

IV.2 String order in the Haldane phase

As an independent validation that the optimized ansatze capture the correct ground-state physics, and not merely the correct energy, I compute the non-local string order parameter

Cstr​(r)=⟨S0z​(∏k=1r−1ei​π​Skz)​Srz⟩C_{\mathrm{str}}(r)\;=\;\left\langle S^{z}_{0}\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{r-1}e^{i\pi S^{z}_{k}}\right)\!S^{z}_{r}\right\rangle (16)

for integer-spin chains in the Haldane phase. The Haldane phase is characterized by a finite gap above the ground state and by a nontrivial topological order whose signature is precisely the saturation of Cstr​(r)C_{\mathrm{str}}(r) to a nonzero value at large rr, together with fractionalized edge degrees of freedom that escape detection by any local order parameter. Since RBMpow performed quite well in estimating the energies in the previous cases, I have used this ansatz only for this purpose, limited by computational resources. I see that RBMpow reproduces the correct plateau (Fig.2), confirming that the nonlinear ansatze recover Haldane phase qualitatively and not just its energy.
In both cases of spin 1 and 2, the curves exhibit the characteristic shape qualitatively imposed by the periodic geometry. The r=0r=0 point is not a string correlation but the on-site moment ⟨(Sz)2⟩\langle(S^{z})^{2}\rangle, and is shown only for reference. A non-vanishing, distance-independent plateau in the bulk regime (r∼N/3r\sim N/3 to 2​N/32N/3), where the endpoints are well separated along both arcs, is the signature of the Haldane phase, in which, the ground state has long-range string order even though conventional spin-spin correlations decay.

For the spin-1 chain (Fig. 2(a)), the KAN ansatz reproduces the DMRG result quantitatively although not very accurately. It displays a clean bulk plateau at around |Ostringz|≈0.31|O_{\mathrm{string}}^{z}|\approx 0.31 compared to the reported value 0.370.37, obtained by the DMRG. Nvertheless, the KAN-NQS curve tracks the DMRG reference across the full range of separations. thus faithfully capturing the hidden string order of the spin-1 Haldane phase.
For the spin-2 chain (Fig. 2(b)), the KAN ansatz reproduces the same qualitative structure, but with a substantially suppressed magnitude, roughly an order of magnitude below the obtained DMRG value. I found that this suppression is accompanied by a corresponding deficit in the local moment: the KAN state yields ⟨(Sz)2⟩≈1.76\langle(S^{z})^{2}\rangle\approx 1.76 per site, against the exact value of 2.02.0. This discrepancy arises even though the variational energy agrees with the DMRG reference to better than 10−310^{-3}. Upon continued optimization at fixed network architecture, the local moment drifts upward toward the exact value while the energy remains essentially unchanged. Hence, the underestimation of the string order and local moment reflects the markedly slower convergence of these nonlocal observables under variational optimization, rather than an intrinsic inability of the KAN ansatz to represent Haldane order.

V Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for the spin-11 Heisenberg chain

V.1 KAN variational wavefunction

The RBM benchmarks of Sec.IV establish the nonlinear scalar encoding as the more efficient categorical construction at small system sizes. I now turn to KANs as a strictly more expressive realization of the same idea, and I push the comparison to a system that is well beyond the reach of exact diagonalization: the spin-11 Heisenberg chain on N=24N=24 sites with periodic boundary conditions.

The Kolmogorov-Arnold superposition theorem states that any continuous multivariate function can be expressed as a finite superposition of univariate functions [12]. Treating the map from a configuration to its (log-)amplitude as such a function, one may write

log⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈)≡log⁡ΨKAN​(𝝈)=∑q=12​N+1Φq​(∑p=1Nϕq,p​(σp)),\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma})\;\equiv\;\log\Psi_{\mathrm{KAN}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{q=1}^{2N+1}\Phi_{q}\!\left(\sum_{p=1}^{N}\phi_{q,p}(\sigma_{p})\right), (17)

with inner univariate functions ϕq,p\phi_{q,p} and outer univariate functions Φq\Phi_{q}. While the theorem guarantees the existence of such a decomposition, it prescribes neither the explicit form of ϕ\phi and Φ\Phi nor a means of constructing them. A KAN resolves this by replacing each univariate function with a learnable parametrized family, so that Eq. (17) is approximated by a trainable network,

log⁡ΨKA​(𝝈)≈log⁡ΨKAN​(𝝈,𝜽),\log\Psi_{\mathrm{KA}}(\bm{\sigma})\;\approx\;\log\Psi_{\mathrm{KAN}}(\bm{\sigma};\bm{\theta}), (18)

whose parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are optimized variationally. Crucially, the inner functions act directly on the raw scalar site variable σp\sigma_{p}, so no expansion of the local state into a dd-dimensional indicator vector is required.
Recently, Shamim et al.[20] a KAN-based NQS (KAN-NQS) ansatz with learnable sinusoidal edge functions, and demonstrated its accuracy on the ground-state energies, fidelities, and correlation functions of the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising, anisotropic Heisenberg, and J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} models. Their study, however, was confined almost entirely to spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} systems, leaving open the question of how KAN ansätze behave for higher local dimensions such as spin-SS (S>12S>\tfrac{1}{2}) or qq-state Potts models.

V.2 Architectures

I compare two NQS ansatze of comparable parameter count:

  1. 1.

    a one-hot encoded Multilayer Perceptron (OH-MLP), in which each site ii is represented by a 33-dimensional indicator vector 𝒗i∈{0,1}3\bm{v}_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{3}, the full 3​N3N-dimensional input is fed through two hidden layers of width WW with smooth nonlinear activations, and the network output gives log⁡Ψ\log\Psi as a complex scalar;

  2. 2.

    a two-layer KAN-NQS ansatz, acting on the raw scalar inputs σi∈{−1,0,1}\sigma_{i}\in\{-1,0,1\} .

Both networks output a complex-valued log⁡Ψ\log\Psi, and both are trained using the Minimal step SR with the same spin-conserved sampler with the he total SzS^{z} is constrained to zero, the similar variable diagonal shift 10−310^{-3}-10−210^{-2}, and also the gradual decreasing of the learning rate so that values do not rise near the convergence schedule of the learning rate γ\gamma.

The learnable sinusoidal basis functions are used in the KAN in this work, following their first introduction in [19] and subsequent use in [20]. One layer of SineKAN is written as a sum of sinusoidal basis functions, similar to the ones mentioned in Eq. 3 section IIE. The model learns amplitudes Ai​j​kA_{ijk} frequencies ωk\omega_{k} over a grid of fixed phases ωj​k\omega_{jk}, The base functional form of the sines are fixed.

V.3 Variational energies and convergence

VMC optimizations were performed with the SR for around 1600 samples per epoch. The KAN-NQS and OH-MLP ansatze were The KAN-NQS of layer dimensions 24-48-1m haveing Np≈3500N_{p}\approx 3500 parameters reaches a lower variational energy than the OH-MLP, having around Np≈2000N_{p}\approx 2000 (Fig. 3). On the 24-site chain the KAN energy is within ∼10−3\sim\!10^{-3} (relative error) of the DMRG reference, while the OH-MLP plateaus at a visibly higher energy, which can be clearly attributed to the VMC optimzation. The advantage is robust across multiple random initializations and across the range of widths I tested. This is attributed to the more to the more compact encoding of the local Hilbert space (a single scalar input per site rather than three indicators) and to the flexibility of the learnable per-edge nonlinearity, which allows the network to adapt its basis to the structure of the wave function rather than committing to a fixed embedding chosen by the practitioner. The rugged optimization landscape in case of the OH-MLP due to more number of parameters makes inhibits it from reaching the global minimum.

V.4 SR spectrum and quantum geometric tensor

A similar pattern observed in the RBM benchmarks reappears here, as shown in (Fig. 3(b)): The SineKAN spectrum is concentrated in the range 10−310^{-3}–10410^{4}, with a well-populated set of large eigenvalues and a subdominant tail near 10−1410^{-14}. The one-hot MLP spectrum is displaced downward by several orders of magnitude: its dominant peak lies at λ∼10−7\lambda\sim 10^{-7}, its largest eigenvalues do not exceed λ∼100\lambda\sim 10^{0}, and a substantial fraction of its density occupies a lobe near 10−2410^{-24} that has no counterpart in the KAN spectrum.

The relevant comparison is not the absolute position of these spectra, which depends on the parameterization, but the fraction of directions that are resolvable given the sampling budget(2048 in this case). Since SS is estimated stochastically, eigenvalues below λmax/Ns\lambda_{\max}/\sqrt{N_{s}} are not distinguishable from estimator noise and cannot be reliably inverted by the natural-gradient preconditioner. The SineKAN, although has a sizeable population of directions clustered around machine precision, still it has significant number of eigenvalues clustered around 10−​510^{-}5 to 10310^{3}. In contrast, OH-MLP not only has its bulk lying several orders of magnitude below (10−​1010^{-}10 to 10−​510^{-}5), but aslo has a wide spreading of the sprectrum. Thus it distributes its Np≈3500N_{p}\approx 3500 parameters across a variational manifold whose curvature is, in most directions, too weak to be resolved at this sample count, while the KAN’s more compact parameterization (Np≈2000N_{p}\approx 2000) concentrates the geometry into directions that remain well conditioned.

VI KAN ansatz for the 55-state quantum Potts model

The categorical-input perspective makes no use of the spin-SS structure of the Hilbert space: it applies equally to any local alphabet of size dd. Unlike spin variables, the local Potts states carry no intrinsic algebraic structure. The (2​S+1)(2S+1) states of a spin-SS degree of freedom are eigenstates of SzS^{z} connected by the ladder operators S±S^{\pm}, which impose a natural ordering. On the other hand, the qq Potts states, are mutually equivalent and equidistant, most naturally represented as the vertices of a regular (q−1)(q-1)-simplex (an equilateral triangle for q=3q=3, a tetrahedron for q=4q=4). No state lies ”between” any other. The only invariant distinction is whether two sites occupy the same state or not. I exploit this to test the KAN ansatz on the one-dimensional quantum Potts model with q=5q=5 in a transverse field, Eq.(15). This model has two distinguishing features that make it a stringent benchmark for NQS:

  1. 1.

    the local Hilbert space has dimension d=q=5d=q=5, with no natural ordering of the local states: unlike the Heisenberg spins. There is no spin-SzS^{z} axis to anchor a linear encoding.

  2. 2.

    for q≥5q\geq 5, the transition between the symmetry-broken “ordered” phase (Γ≪J\Gamma\ll J) and the paramagnetic phase (Γ≫J\Gamma\gg J) is of first order [21], characterized by a discontinuous jump in the magnetization rather than by a continuous critical point.

VI.1 KAN-NQS for Potts variables

I use the same KAN-NQS architecture as in Sec. V, with the input alphabet now taken to be σi∈{0,1,2,3,4}\sigma_{i}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}.

VI.2 Representation cost of the Potts coincidence feature

The diagonal term of the qq-state quantum Potts Hamiltonian is built from the coincidence feature

δσi​σj={1σi=σj,0σi≠σj,σi,σj∈{0,1,…,q−1}.\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=\begin{cases}1&\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{j},\\ 0&\sigma_{i}\neq\sigma_{j},\end{cases}\qquad\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j}\in\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}.

Here I make precise the cost of reconstructing δ\delta from a single-site scalar encoding σ↦sσ∈ℝ\sigma\mapsto s_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}. It is easy top see that it forces a cost that grows linearly in qq in bilinear, or nested two-layer architectures.

Throughout, let M∈ℝq×qM\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q} denote the coincidence matrix Ma​b=δa​bM_{ab}=\delta_{ab}. Then M=IqM=I_{q}, the q×qq\times q identity, and in particular rank⁡M=q\operatorname{rank}M=q. This single fact drives the lower bounds below.

Proposition 1 (Cost of the coincidence feature under a scalar encoding).

Let q≥3q\geq 3, let σ↦sσ∈ℝ\sigma\mapsto s_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R} be any scalar encoding of the qq Potts states, and let M∈ℝq×qM\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q} be the coincidence matrix Ma​b=δa​bM_{ab}=\delta_{ab}. Then:

  1. (i)

    (Additive forms fail.) There exist no univariate f,g:ℝ→ℝf,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} with δσi​σj=f⁡(sσi)+g⁡(sσj)\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=f(s_{\sigma_{i}})+g(s_{\sigma_{j}}).

  2. (ii)

    (Bilinear forms cost qq.) If δσi​σj=∑k=1rak​ϕk​(sσi)​ψk​(sσj)\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=\sum_{k=1}^{r}a_{k}\,\phi_{k}(s_{\sigma_{i}})\,\psi_{k}(s_{\sigma_{j}}) for univariate ϕk,ψk\phi_{k},\psi_{k}, then r≥qr\geq q, and r=qr=q is attained.

  3. (iii)

    (Nested sinusoidal forms cost ⌈(q−1)/2⌉\lceil(q-1)/2\rceil.) If

    δσi​σj=c0+∑t=1TAt​sin⁡(αt​sσi+βt​sσj+φt),\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=c_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_{t}\sin\!\big(\alpha_{t}s_{\sigma_{i}}+\beta_{t}s_{\sigma_{j}}+\varphi_{t}\big), (19)

    then T≥⌈(q−1)/2⌉T\geq\lceil(q-1)/2\rceil, and this value is attained.

Proof.

All three statements follow from a single observation. Each candidate construction writes MM as a sum of elementary blocks, and the rank of a sum never exceeds the sum of the ranks; since M=IqM=I_{q} , the q×qq\times q identity, has rank⁡M=q\operatorname{rank}M=q, it suffices to bound the rank of one block and count.

Rank of the blocks. Write 𝟏=(1,…,1)⊤\bm{1}=(1,\dots,1)^{\!\top}.

  • •

    An additive block has entries f⁡(sa)+g⁡(sb)f(s_{a})+g(s_{b}), i.e. 𝒇​𝟏⊤+𝟏​𝒈⊤\bm{f}\bm{1}^{\!\top}+\bm{1}\bm{g}^{\!\top} with fa=f⁡(sa)f_{a}=f(s_{a}), gb=g⁡(sb)g_{b}=g(s_{b}): rank at most 22.

  • •

    A bilinear block has entries ϕ⁡(sa)​ψ​(sb)\phi(s_{a})\psi(s_{b}), i.e. the outer product ϕ​𝝍⊤\bm{\phi}\bm{\psi}^{\!\top}: rank at most 11.

  • •

    A sinusoidal block has entries sin⁡(α​sa+β​sb+φ)\sin(\alpha s_{a}+\beta s_{b}+\varphi). Setting ua=α​sa+φu_{a}=\alpha s_{a}+\varphi, vb=β​sbv_{b}=\beta s_{b} and using sin⁡(u+v)=sin⁡u​cos⁡v+cos⁡u​sin⁡v\sin(u+v)=\sin u\cos v+\cos u\sin v gives

    [sin⁡(α​sa+β​sb+φ)]a​b=𝒑​𝒓⊤+𝒔​𝒘⊤,\big[\sin(\alpha s_{a}+\beta s_{b}+\varphi)\big]_{ab}=\bm{p}\,\bm{r}^{\!\top}+\bm{s}\,\bm{w}^{\!\top}, (20)

    with pa=sin⁡uap_{a}=\sin u_{a}, sa′=cos⁡uas_{a}^{\prime}=\cos u_{a}, rb=cos⁡vbr_{b}=\cos v_{b}, wb=sin⁡vbw_{b}=\sin v_{b}: rank at most 22. The bound is independent of α,β,φ\alpha,\beta,\varphi and of the encoding, and reflects the two conjugate characters e±i⁡(α​sa+β​sb)e^{\pm i(\alpha s_{a}+\beta s_{b})} carried by a real sinusoid.

  • •

    A constant block is c0​𝟏𝟏⊤c_{0}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}: rank at most 11.

Counting. For (i), a single additive block gives q≤2q\leq 2, contradicting q≥3q\geq 3. For (ii), rr bilinear blocks give q≤rq\leq r. For (iii), one constant block and TT sinusoidal blocks give q≤1+2​Tq\leq 1+2T, i.e. T≥(q−1)/2T\geq(q-1)/2, and T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} forces T≥⌈(q−1)/2⌉T\geq\lceil(q-1)/2\rceil.

Attainability. Take sσ=σs_{\sigma}=\sigma and start from the character resolution of the delta on ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q}, with ω=e2​π​i/q\omega=e^{2\pi i/q}:

δσi​σj=1q​∑k=0q−1ωk⁡(σi−σj)=∑k=0q−11q​(ωk​σi)​(ω−k​σj),\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\omega^{k(\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{j})}=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\frac{1}{q}\big(\omega^{k\sigma_{i}}\big)\big(\omega^{-k\sigma_{j}}\big), (21)

which is exactly the bilinear form of (ii) with r=qr=q, ak=1/qa_{k}=1/q, ϕk​(s)=ωk​s\phi_{k}(s)=\omega^{ks}, ψk​(s)=ω−k​s\psi_{k}(s)=\omega^{-ks}. Since δ\delta is real, the sine parts cancel under k↔q−kk\leftrightarrow q-k and δσi​σj=1q​∑k=0q−1cos⁡(2​π​kq​m)\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}\cos\!\big(\tfrac{2\pi k}{q}m\big) with m=σi−σjm=\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{j}. Because mm is an integer and the cosine is even, the summands at kk and q−kq-k are the same function, so each distinct cosine occurs twice except for the self-paired indices k=0k=0 and, for even qq, k=q/2k=q/2. Merging duplicates,

δσi​σj={1q+2q​∑k=1⌈q/2⌉−1cos⁡(2​π​kq​(σi−σj)),for odd ​q,2q​∑k=1q/2cos⁡(2​π​kq​(σi−σj)),for even ​q.\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{q}+\frac{2}{q}\sum_{k=1}^{\lceil q/2\rceil-1}\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{q}(\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{j})\right),&\text{for odd }q,\\[6.45831pt] \displaystyle\frac{2}{q}\sum_{k=1}^{q/2}\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{q}(\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{j})\right),&\text{for even }q.\end{cases} (22)

∎

The Hamiltonian Eq. (15) is implemented in NetKet as a sum of local operators acting on the 55-dimensional on-site Hilbert space, and I use a Metropolis sampler with single-site updates. For each value of Γ/J\Gamma/J I train an independent KAN-NQS with matched architecture, and I report converged values of the magnetization

⟨M⟩=1N​⟨∑icos⁡(2​πq​ni)⟩,\langle M\rangle\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\Bigl\langle\sum_{i}\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{q}\,n_{i}\right)\Bigr\rangle, (23)

where ni∈{0,…,q−1}n_{i}\in\{0,\dots,q-1\} labels the on-site Potts state. As reference, I run DMRG on the same lattice with bond dimension χ=400\chi=400 in the ITensor implementation [9].

VI.3 Phase transition and order-parameter jump

Figure 4 shows the order parameter ⟨M⟩\langle M\rangle obtained from the KAN ansatz across the Γ\Gamma-driven transition of the q=5q=5 quantum Potts chain at L=40L=40 with PBC, together with the DMRG reference computed for the same Hamiltonian. Both calculations include symmetry-breaking pinning fields of strength hp=1.0h_{\rm p}=1.0 applied to the two boundary sites, which select a single ordered sector and render the order parameter well defined at finite size. But no information about the location or character of the transition enters the ansatz. The ansatz reproduces the qualitative structure of the transition, notably, ⟨M⟩≃1\langle M\rangle\simeq 1 throughout the ordered phase, a rapid collapse near Γ/J≈0.46\Gamma/J\approx 0.46 that agrees with the DMRG result to within the resolution of our Γ\Gamma grid, and ⟨M⟩≲0.02\langle M\rangle\lesssim 0.02 deep in the disordered phase. The agreement degrades in a window 0.38≲Γ/J≲0.620.38\lesssim\Gamma/J\lesssim 0.62 surrounding the transition, where the estimates scatter about the DMRG curve by up to ∼0.15\sim 0.15 in |M||M|.
This discrepancy near Γc\Gamma_{c} is expected on physical grounds even in the presence of pinning. The boundary term lifts the qq-fold degeneracy among the ordered states, but it does not remove the near-degeneracy between the selected ordered state and the disordered state, which is intrinsic to the first-order transition and which the pinning field cannot resolve in the bulk of a chain of this length. The two competing states remain separated by a barrier in configuration space, so a Metropolis chain initialized in one of them exchanges with the other only rarely. so the sampled distribution can remain trapped in a single ordered sector even when the true ground state has weight on several. The resulting bias in the stochastic estimates of both the energy gradient and the SR drives the optimization toward a state whose order parameter reflects the sampled sector, particularly when there are competing states that are close in energy.

VI.4 Testing the expressibility of the KAN for Potts variables by Supervised learning

To verify whether this is a discrepancy of sampling and optimization process or a limitation of the KAN parameterization itself, I tried the supervised learning of the KAN with the DMRG ground state, I fit the KAN directly to DMRG ground state ( (supervised learning) at Γ/J=0.48\Gamma/J=0.48, inside the window where the variational estimates of Fig. 4 deviate most strongly from the reference. A large pool of 50000 training samples σ∼|ψD|2\sigma\sim|\psi_{D}|^{2} were drawn and the log⁡ψD​(σ)\log\psi_{D}(\sigma) were evaluated. A validation set of 4096 samples were also drawn independently. So the supervised loss

ℒ=⟨|log⁡ψK​A​N​(σ)−log⁡ψD​(σ)−c|2⟩σ\mathcal{L}\;=\;\big\langle|\,\log\psi_{KAN}(\sigma)-\log\psi_{D}(\sigma)-c\,|^{2}\big\rangle_{\sigma} (24)

was calculated, where cc is set to the batch mean of log⁡ψD−log⁡ψK​A​N\log\psi_{D}-\log\psi_{KAN} at each training epoch. Removing the variational loop eliminates sector trapping by construction, since the training configurations are drawn from the exact ground-state distribution rather than from a Metropolis sampling.

Figure 5 shows the resulting loss curves. The training and validation losses fall by more than an order of magnitude within the first ∼103\sim 10^{3} epochs and thereafter decrease slowly, reaching ℒ≈0.2\mathcal{L}\approx 0.2 at 8×1038\times 10^{3} epochs without having fully converged. The two curves remain separated by a small and approximately constant offset throughout, with no upturn in the validation loss, indicating that the fit is limited by optimization rather than by overfitting to the training configurations: the generalization gap is far smaller than the residual loss itself.

The residual is nonetheless appreciable, corresponding to typical log-amplitude errors of order 0.40.4. This shows that even in the absence of sampling bias the sign- and amplitude-structure of the q=5q=5 ground state near the transition remains difficult to fit quantitatively at this network size and training budget, and identifies the supervised optimization floor as the appropriate target for further architectural refinement.

In short, The combination of (i) accurate energetics, (ii) a correctly reproduced first-order order-parameter jump, and (iii) high overlap fidelity with DMRG demonstrates that a single KAN architecture acting directly on the raw 55-state Potts variable is sufficient to capture the qualitative ground-state physics on both sides of, and across, a strongly first-order quantum phase transition. I am not aware of comparable NQS results for the q≥5q\geq 5 quantum Potts chain in the literature.

VII Conclusion

I have argued that for neural network quantum states applied to systems with local Hilbert space dimension d≥3d\geq 3, quantum spin models with S>12S>\tfrac{1}{2}, qq-state Potts models, and their relatives the relevant design principle is that log⁡Ψ\log\Psi depending on a nonlinear univariate functions of the raw categorical visible variables can also be an efficient ansatze. Together with the labelling freedom of the local basis, this principle was tested om a family of ansatze that include the shallow nonlinear RBMs, the most general possible nonlinear scalar encoding, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks acting on raw spin or Potts inputs.

Numerically, I have verified that on small 22 and 33 Heisenberg chains, nonlinear RBMs reach the ED energy with strictly fewer parameters than the corresponding one-hot RBMs, and for spin-22 the and RBMChe parameterization improves both the energetics and the conditioning of the SR matrix, and for spin-33, the the RBMpow performs better and the the RBMChe lags the most, On the 2424-site spin-11 Heisenberg chain, a KAN ansatz acting on raw spin inputs outperforms a OH-MLP both in variational energy and in SR spectrum quality , since the SR optimization struggles duw to higher parameter count for the OH-MLP. On the one-dimensional q=5q=5 quantum Potts model in a transverse field, the same KAN ansatz reproduces the first-order transition through a discontinuous jump in ⟨M⟩\langle M\rangle as a function of Γ/J\Gamma/J, and attains a ground-state fidelity above 0.990.99 with DMRG reference states on either side of the transition. These results suggest that a better way to “upgrade” a binary NQS to a categorical NQS is not to one-hot encode the inputs, but to allow the log-amplitude to be a nonlinear function of the raw categorical variable. KANs provide a particularly clean realization of this principle and, together with translation- and permutation-symmetric architectures, appear to be a promising substrate for NQS in general-spin and Potts-like quantum systems.

Implications for higher-dimensional and frustrated systems.

The KAN construction extends straightforwardly to two-dimensional lattices and to models with continuous symmetries; in particular, the combination of KAN edge functions with graph-attention layers appears to be a natural ansatz for frustrated J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg models on the square lattice, where competing orders make the optimization landscape especially treacherous. I leave a systematic study to future scope of work.
